title: Star Industries vs. ABC Pvt. Ltd. (2016)
content:
Telangana High Court

Star Industries ... Petitioner/Appellant
Versus
ABC Pvt. Ltd. ... Respondent

Date of Judgment: 17.10.2016

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to writ petition seeking protection of fundamental rights - article 19.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court writ petition seeking protection of freedom of speech, expression, assembly. The case involves important questions of law concerning fundamental rights - article 19 and its interpretation in the context of freedom of speech, expression, assembly.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding freedom of speech, expression, assembly. The petitioner contends that writ petition seeking protection of freedom of speech, expression, assembly is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Fundamental Rights - Article 19 in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that freedom of speech, expression, assembly are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Fundamental Rights - Article 19.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Fundamental Rights - Article 19. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that freedom of speech, expression, assembly are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that writ petition seeking protection of freedom of speech, expression, assembly must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Fundamental Rights - Article 19 must be interpreted in light of freedom of speech, expression, assembly.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to acquittal in case involving domestic violence act.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court acquittal in case involving protection from domestic violence. The case involves important questions of law concerning domestic violence act and its interpretation in the context of protection from domestic violence.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding protection from domestic violence. The petitioner contends that acquittal in case involving protection from domestic violence is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Domestic Violence Act in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that protection from domestic violence are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Domestic Violence Act.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Domestic Violence Act. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that protection from domestic violence are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that acquittal in case involving protection from domestic violence must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Domestic Violence Act must be interpreted in light of protection from domestic violence.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to anticipatory bail for allegations of ipc section 302.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court anticipatory bail for allegations of murder, homicide, intention to kill. The case involves important questions of law concerning ipc section 302 and its interpretation in the context of murder, homicide, intention to kill.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding murder, homicide, intention to kill. The petitioner contends that anticipatory bail for allegations of murder, homicide, intention to kill is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of IPC Section 302 in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that murder, homicide, intention to kill are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning IPC Section 302.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to IPC Section 302. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that murder, homicide, intention to kill are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that anticipatory bail for allegations of murder, homicide, intention to kill must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. IPC Section 302 must be interpreted in light of murder, homicide, intention to kill.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

title: Sanjay Joshi vs. Union of India (1982)
content:
Telangana High Court

Sanjay Joshi ... Petitioner/Appellant
Versus
Union of India ... Respondent

Date of Judgment: 23.01.1982

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to injunction against tort - negligence.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court injunction against duty of care, damages, compensation. The case involves important questions of law concerning tort - negligence and its interpretation in the context of duty of care, damages, compensation.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding duty of care, damages, compensation. The petitioner contends that injunction against duty of care, damages, compensation is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Tort - Negligence in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that duty of care, damages, compensation are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Tort - Negligence.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Tort - Negligence. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that duty of care, damages, compensation are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that injunction against duty of care, damages, compensation must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Tort - Negligence must be interpreted in light of duty of care, damages, compensation.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to challenge to validity of marriage validity.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court challenge to validity of void marriage, voidable marriage. The case involves important questions of law concerning marriage validity and its interpretation in the context of void marriage, voidable marriage.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding void marriage, voidable marriage. The petitioner contends that challenge to validity of void marriage, voidable marriage is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Marriage Validity in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that void marriage, voidable marriage are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Marriage Validity.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Marriage Validity. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that void marriage, voidable marriage are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that challenge to validity of void marriage, voidable marriage must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Marriage Validity must be interpreted in light of void marriage, voidable marriage.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

Telangana High Court

Arun Desai ... Petitioner/Appellant
Versus
Income Tax Department ... Respondent

Date of Judgment: 14.12.2024

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to protection order for maintenance under crpc 125.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court protection order for wife maintenance, child support. The case involves important questions of law concerning maintenance under crpc 125 and its interpretation in the context of wife maintenance, child support.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding wife maintenance, child support. The petitioner contends that protection order for wife maintenance, child support is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Maintenance under CrPC 125 in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that wife maintenance, child support are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Maintenance under CrPC 125.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Maintenance under CrPC 125. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that wife maintenance, child support are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that protection order for wife maintenance, child support must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Maintenance under CrPC 125 must be interpreted in light of wife maintenance, child support.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

title: Bharath Manufacturing vs. State of Maharashtra (1988)
content:
Delhi High Court

Bharath Manufacturing ... Petitioner/Appellant
Versus
State of Maharashtra ... Respondent

Date of Judgment: 31.12.1988

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to competition commission investigation into sebi regulations.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court competition commission investigation into insider trading, market manipulation. The case involves important questions of law concerning sebi regulations and its interpretation in the context of insider trading, market manipulation.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding insider trading, market manipulation. The petitioner contends that competition commission investigation into insider trading, market manipulation is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of SEBI Regulations in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that insider trading, market manipulation are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning SEBI Regulations.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to SEBI Regulations. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that insider trading, market manipulation are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that competition commission investigation into insider trading, market manipulation must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. SEBI Regulations must be interpreted in light of insider trading, market manipulation.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

Telangana High Court

ABC Pvt. Ltd. ... Petitioner/Appellant
Versus
Star Industries ... Respondent

Date of Judgment: 18.06.2022

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to competition commission investigation into corporate governance.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court competition commission investigation into director duties, fiduciary obligations. The case involves important questions of law concerning corporate governance and its interpretation in the context of director duties, fiduciary obligations.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding director duties, fiduciary obligations. The petitioner contends that competition commission investigation into director duties, fiduciary obligations is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Corporate Governance in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that director duties, fiduciary obligations are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Corporate Governance.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Corporate Governance. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that director duties, fiduciary obligations are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that competition commission investigation into director duties, fiduciary obligations must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Corporate Governance must be interpreted in light of director duties, fiduciary obligations.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to dispute regarding reinstatement after contract labor act.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court dispute regarding reinstatement after principal employer liability, regularization. The case involves important questions of law concerning contract labor act and its interpretation in the context of principal employer liability, regularization.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding principal employer liability, regularization. The petitioner contends that dispute regarding reinstatement after principal employer liability, regularization is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Contract Labor Act in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that principal employer liability, regularization are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Contract Labor Act.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Contract Labor Act. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that principal employer liability, regularization are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that dispute regarding reinstatement after principal employer liability, regularization must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Contract Labor Act must be interpreted in light of principal employer liability, regularization.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

Versus

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to application for benefits under trade unions act.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court application for benefits under recognition, collective bargaining. The case involves important questions of law concerning trade unions act and its interpretation in the context of recognition, collective bargaining.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding recognition, collective bargaining. The petitioner contends that application for benefits under recognition, collective bargaining is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Trade Unions Act in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that recognition, collective bargaining are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Trade Unions Act.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Trade Unions Act. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that recognition, collective bargaining are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that application for benefits under recognition, collective bargaining must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Trade Unions Act must be interpreted in light of recognition, collective bargaining.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

title: Kavita Nair vs. State of Maharashtra (1996)
content:
Supreme Court of India

Kavita Nair ... Petitioner/Appellant
Versus
State of Maharashtra ... Respondent

Date of Judgment: 18.05.1996

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to dispute regarding reinstatement after contract labor act.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court dispute regarding reinstatement after principal employer liability, regularization. The case involves important questions of law concerning contract labor act and its interpretation in the context of principal employer liability, regularization.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding principal employer liability, regularization. The petitioner contends that dispute regarding reinstatement after principal employer liability, regularization is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Contract Labor Act in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that principal employer liability, regularization are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Contract Labor Act.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Contract Labor Act. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that principal employer liability, regularization are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that dispute regarding reinstatement after principal employer liability, regularization must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Contract Labor Act must be interpreted in light of principal employer liability, regularization.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

Kerala High Court

National Industries ... Petitioner/Appellant
Versus
Sunita Patel ... Respondent

Date of Judgment: 23.12.1997

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to appeal against assessment order for customs act.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court appeal against assessment order for classification of goods, valuation, duty. The case involves important questions of law concerning customs act and its interpretation in the context of classification of goods, valuation, duty.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding classification of goods, valuation, duty. The petitioner contends that appeal against assessment order for classification of goods, valuation, duty is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Customs Act in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that classification of goods, valuation, duty are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Customs Act.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Customs Act. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that classification of goods, valuation, duty are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that appeal against assessment order for classification of goods, valuation, duty must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Customs Act must be interpreted in light of classification of goods, valuation, duty.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

Sd/-
Judge
Kerala High Court

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to challenge to penalty levied for tax refund.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court challenge to penalty levied for delayed refund, interest on refund. The case involves important questions of law concerning tax refund and its interpretation in the context of delayed refund, interest on refund.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding delayed refund, interest on refund. The petitioner contends that challenge to penalty levied for delayed refund, interest on refund is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Tax Refund in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that delayed refund, interest on refund are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Tax Refund.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Tax Refund. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that delayed refund, interest on refund are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that challenge to penalty levied for delayed refund, interest on refund must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Tax Refund must be interpreted in light of delayed refund, interest on refund.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to search and seizure proceedings for income tax act.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court search and seizure proceedings for assessment, penalty, search and seizure. The case involves important questions of law concerning income tax act and its interpretation in the context of assessment, penalty, search and seizure.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding assessment, penalty, search and seizure. The petitioner contends that search and seizure proceedings for assessment, penalty, search and seizure is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Income Tax Act in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that assessment, penalty, search and seizure are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Income Tax Act.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Income Tax Act. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that assessment, penalty, search and seizure are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that search and seizure proceedings for assessment, penalty, search and seizure must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Income Tax Act must be interpreted in light of assessment, penalty, search and seizure.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

The petitioner contends that infringement suit for unauthorized use of reproduction, communication to public is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:

3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that reproduction, communication to public are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Copyright Infringement.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Copyright Infringement. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that reproduction, communication to public are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that infringement suit for unauthorized use of reproduction, communication to public must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Copyright Infringement must be interpreted in light of reproduction, communication to public.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

Tech Solutions India ... Petitioner/Appellant
Versus
Rahul Gupta ... Respondent

Date of Judgment: 13.02.1985

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to opposition to registration of trade secrets.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court opposition to registration of confidential information, unfair competition. The case involves important questions of law concerning trade secrets and its interpretation in the context of confidential information, unfair competition.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding confidential information, unfair competition. The petitioner contends that opposition to registration of confidential information, unfair competition is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Trade Secrets in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that confidential information, unfair competition are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Trade Secrets.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Trade Secrets. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that confidential information, unfair competition are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that opposition to registration of confidential information, unfair competition must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Trade Secrets must be interpreted in light of confidential information, unfair competition.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

content:

Versus

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to licensing dispute concerning licensing disputes.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court licensing dispute concerning royalty, breach of license. The case involves important questions of law concerning licensing disputes and its interpretation in the context of royalty, breach of license.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding royalty, breach of license. The petitioner contends that licensing dispute concerning royalty, breach of license is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Licensing Disputes in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that royalty, breach of license are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Licensing Disputes.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Licensing Disputes. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that royalty, breach of license are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that licensing dispute concerning royalty, breach of license must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Licensing Disputes must be interpreted in light of royalty, breach of license.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

content:
Punjab and Haryana High Court

Versus
Sunita Patel ... Respondent

Date of Judgment: 11.09.1985

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to patent invalidity challenge based on domain name disputes.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court patent invalidity challenge based on cybersquatting, trademark rights. The case involves important questions of law concerning domain name disputes and its interpretation in the context of cybersquatting, trademark rights.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding cybersquatting, trademark rights. The petitioner contends that patent invalidity challenge based on cybersquatting, trademark rights is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Domain Name Disputes in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that cybersquatting, trademark rights are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Domain Name Disputes.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Domain Name Disputes. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that cybersquatting, trademark rights are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that patent invalidity challenge based on cybersquatting, trademark rights must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Domain Name Disputes must be interpreted in light of cybersquatting, trademark rights.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

title: Tech Solutions India vs. Tech Solutions India (2022)
content:
Calcutta High Court

Tech Solutions India ... Petitioner/Appellant
Versus
Tech Solutions India ... Respondent

Date of Judgment: 06.10.2022

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to licensing dispute concerning copyright infringement.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court licensing dispute concerning reproduction, communication to public. The case involves important questions of law concerning copyright infringement and its interpretation in the context of reproduction, communication to public.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding reproduction, communication to public. The petitioner contends that licensing dispute concerning reproduction, communication to public is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Copyright Infringement in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that reproduction, communication to public are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Copyright Infringement.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Copyright Infringement. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that reproduction, communication to public are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that licensing dispute concerning reproduction, communication to public must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Copyright Infringement must be interpreted in light of reproduction, communication to public.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

content:
Karnataka High Court

Vikram Mehta ... Petitioner/Appellant
Versus
Vikram Mehta ... Respondent

Date of Judgment: 16.09.1996

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to infringement suit for unauthorized use of copyright infringement.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court infringement suit for unauthorized use of reproduction, communication to public. The case involves important questions of law concerning copyright infringement and its interpretation in the context of reproduction, communication to public.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding reproduction, communication to public. The petitioner contends that infringement suit for unauthorized use of reproduction, communication to public is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Copyright Infringement in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that reproduction, communication to public are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Copyright Infringement.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Copyright Infringement. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that reproduction, communication to public are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that infringement suit for unauthorized use of reproduction, communication to public must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Copyright Infringement must be interpreted in light of reproduction, communication to public.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

Punjab and Haryana High Court

ABC Pvt. Ltd. ... Petitioner/Appellant
Versus
State of Delhi ... Respondent

Date of Judgment: 19.09.1985

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to insurance claim rejection for real estate complaints.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court insurance claim rejection for builder delay, deviation from plan. The case involves important questions of law concerning real estate complaints and its interpretation in the context of builder delay, deviation from plan.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding builder delay, deviation from plan. The petitioner contends that insurance claim rejection for builder delay, deviation from plan is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Real Estate Complaints in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that builder delay, deviation from plan are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Real Estate Complaints.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Real Estate Complaints. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that builder delay, deviation from plan are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that insurance claim rejection for builder delay, deviation from plan must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Real Estate Complaints must be interpreted in light of builder delay, deviation from plan.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

Bombay High Court

Anjali Verma ... Petitioner/Appellant
Versus
Kavita Nair ... Respondent

Date of Judgment: 03.10.2004

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to claim for compensation due to deficiency in service.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court claim for compensation due to negligence, unfair trade practice. The case involves important questions of law concerning deficiency in service and its interpretation in the context of negligence, unfair trade practice.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding negligence, unfair trade practice. The petitioner contends that claim for compensation due to negligence, unfair trade practice is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Deficiency in Service in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that negligence, unfair trade practice are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Deficiency in Service.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Deficiency in Service. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that negligence, unfair trade practice are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that claim for compensation due to negligence, unfair trade practice must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Deficiency in Service must be interpreted in light of negligence, unfair trade practice.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to claim for compensation due to defective goods.

3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that product liability, replacement, refund are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Defective Goods.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Defective Goods. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that product liability, replacement, refund are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that claim for compensation due to product liability, replacement, refund must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Defective Goods must be interpreted in light of product liability, replacement, refund.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

Bombay High Court

Rajesh Kumar ... Petitioner/Appellant
Versus
Kavita Nair ... Respondent

Date of Judgment: 31.10.2017

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to NGT proceedings for violation of environment protection act.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court NGT proceedings for violation of pollution control, environmental clearance. The case involves important questions of law concerning environment protection act and its interpretation in the context of pollution control, environmental clearance.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding pollution control, environmental clearance. The petitioner contends that NGT proceedings for violation of pollution control, environmental clearance is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Environment Protection Act in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that pollution control, environmental clearance are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Environment Protection Act.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Environment Protection Act. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that pollution control, environmental clearance are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that NGT proceedings for violation of pollution control, environmental clearance must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Environment Protection Act must be interpreted in light of pollution control, environmental clearance.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

Versus
Arun Desai ... Respondent

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to enforcement of environmental norms in forest conservation.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court enforcement of environmental norms in forest land diversion, wildlife protection. The case involves important questions of law concerning forest conservation and its interpretation in the context of forest land diversion, wildlife protection.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding forest land diversion, wildlife protection. The petitioner contends that enforcement of environmental norms in forest land diversion, wildlife protection is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Forest Conservation in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that forest land diversion, wildlife protection are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Forest Conservation.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Forest Conservation. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that forest land diversion, wildlife protection are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that enforcement of environmental norms in forest land diversion, wildlife protection must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Forest Conservation must be interpreted in light of forest land diversion, wildlife protection.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to NGT proceedings for violation of environment protection act.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court NGT proceedings for violation of pollution control, environmental clearance. The case involves important questions of law concerning environment protection act and its interpretation in the context of pollution control, environmental clearance.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding pollution control, environmental clearance. The petitioner contends that NGT proceedings for violation of pollution control, environmental clearance is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Environment Protection Act in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that pollution control, environmental clearance are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Environment Protection Act.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Environment Protection Act. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that pollution control, environmental clearance are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that NGT proceedings for violation of pollution control, environmental clearance must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Environment Protection Act must be interpreted in light of pollution control, environmental clearance.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

content:
Supreme Court of India

Sunita Patel ... Petitioner/Appellant
Versus
Kavita Nair ... Respondent

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to challenge to environmental clearance for coastal zone regulation.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court challenge to environmental clearance for CRZ violations, coastal protection. The case involves important questions of law concerning coastal zone regulation and its interpretation in the context of CRZ violations, coastal protection.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding CRZ violations, coastal protection. The petitioner contends that challenge to environmental clearance for CRZ violations, coastal protection is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Coastal Zone Regulation in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that CRZ violations, coastal protection are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Coastal Zone Regulation.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Coastal Zone Regulation. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that CRZ violations, coastal protection are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that challenge to environmental clearance for CRZ violations, coastal protection must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Coastal Zone Regulation must be interpreted in light of CRZ violations, coastal protection.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

title: Rajesh Kumar vs. Union of India (2009)

Gujarat High Court

Rajesh Kumar ... Petitioner/Appellant
Versus
Union of India ... Respondent

Date of Judgment: 22.11.2009

JUDGMENT

This matter pertains to PIL for environmental protection regarding coastal zone regulation.

FACTS:
The petitioner has approached this Court PIL for environmental protection regarding CRZ violations, coastal protection. The case involves important questions of law concerning coastal zone regulation and its interpretation in the context of CRZ violations, coastal protection.

The facts briefly stated are that the petitioner and respondent were involved in a dispute regarding CRZ violations, coastal protection. The petitioner contends that PIL for environmental protection regarding CRZ violations, coastal protection is necessary to protect their legal rights and interests.

ISSUES:
1. Whether the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for relief?
2. What is the correct interpretation of Coastal Zone Regulation in the present circumstances?
3. What relief, if any, is the petitioner entitled to?

CONTENTIONS:
The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that CRZ violations, coastal protection are essential elements that need to be considered. Reference was made to the relevant legal provisions concerning Coastal Zone Regulation.

The learned counsel for the respondent, on the other hand, contended that the case lacks merit and should be dismissed.

LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
The case requires examination of legal principles relating to Coastal Zone Regulation. The relevant statutory provisions and judicial precedents have been carefully considered.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS:
After hearing the learned counsels and examining the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that CRZ violations, coastal protection are crucial factors in determining the outcome.

The principles of natural justice require that PIL for environmental protection regarding CRZ violations, coastal protection must be done in accordance with established legal principles.

CONCLUSION:
In view of the above discussion and considering the totality of circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that the petition/appeal has merit.

HELD:
1. The petition/appeal is allowed.
2. Coastal Zone Regulation must be interpreted in light of CRZ violations, coastal protection.
3. Appropriate relief is granted to the petitioner.
4. Parties to bear their own costs.

The judgment is pronounced in open court.

The  petitioner was issued a passport on June 1, 1976  under
the

.  On the 4th	of  July  1977,	 the
petitioner received a letter dated 2nd July, 1977, from	 the

was  decided  by  the Government of  India  to	impound	 her
passport under
s. 10(3)(c)
of the Act "in public  interest".
The petitioner was required to surrender her passport within
7  days	 from the receipt of that  letter.   The  petitioner
immediately  addressed	a letter to  the  Regional  Passport
Officer requesting him to furnish a copy of the statement of
reasons for making the order as provided in
s.10(5)
. A reply
was  sent by the Government of India, Ministry	of  External
Affairs	 on  6th  July	1977 stating  inter  alia  that	 the
Government  decided "in the interest of the general  public"
not to furnish her copy of the statement of reasons for	 the
making	of  the order.	The petitioner thereupon  filed	 the
present	 Writ Petition challenging action of the  Government
in-  impounding her passport and declining to  give  reasons
for doing so.
The Act
was enacted on 24-4-67 in view of the
decision of this Court in Satwant Singg Sawhney's case.	 The
position  which obtained prior to the coming into  force  of
the  Act was that there was no law regulating the  issue  of
passports for leaving the shores of India and going  abroad.
The  issue of passport was entirely within the unguided	 and
unchannelled  discretion  of  the  Executive.	In   Satwant

Article 21

decision  was accepted by the Parliament and  the  infirmity

Passports Act, 1967
.  The preamble of the Act shows that  it

J U D G M E N T
Verma, CJI:
This Writ	Petition has  been filed for the enforcement
of the	fundamental rights  of working	women under
Articles
14
, 19
and
21
of the	Constitution of India in view of the
prevailing climate in which the violation of these rights is
not uncommon.  With the increasing awareness and emphasis on
gender justice,	 there is  increase in	the effort  to guard
such violations;  and the  resentment towards  incidents  of
sexual harassment  is also  increasing. The present petition
has been  brought  as  a  class	 action	 by  certain  social
activists and  NGOs with  the  aim  of	focussing  attention
towards this  societal aberration,  and assisting in finding
suitable methods  for realisation  of the  true	 concept  of
'gender equality';  and	 to  prevent  sexual  harassment  of
working women  in all  work places through judicial process,
to fill the vacuum in existing legislation.
The  immediate  cause  for	 the  filing  of  this	writ
petition is  an incident  of alleged  brutal  gang  rape  of
social worker  in a  village of	 Rajasthan. That incident is
the subject  matter of	a separate  criminal action  and  no
further mention	 of it,	 by us,	 is necessary.	The incident
reveals the  hazards to which a working woman may be exposed
and the depravity to which sexual harassment can degenerate;
and the	 urgency for  safeguards by an alternative mechanism
in the	absence of  legislative measures.  In the absence of
legislative measures,  the need	 is  to	 find  an  effective
alternative mechanism  to fulfil this felt and urgent social
need.
Each  such	  incident  results   in  violation  of	 the
fundamental rights  of 'Gender	Equality' and  the 'Right of
Life and Liberty'. It is clear violation of the rights under
Articles 14
,  15
and
21
of Constitution. One of the logical
consequences of	 such an  incident is  also the violation of
the victim's  fundamental right	 under
Article	19(1)(g)
'to
practice any  profession or  to carry  out  any	 occupation,
trade or  business'. Such violations, therefore, attract the
remedy	under
Article	32
for	 the  enforcement  of  these
fundamental rights of women. This class action under
Article
32
of  the Constitution	 is  for  this	reason.	 A  writ  of
mandamus in  such a  siltation, if  it is  to be  effective,
needs to be accompanied by directions for prevention; as the
violation of  fundamental rights of this kind is a recurring
phenomenon.  The   fundamental	right	to  carry   on	 any
occupation, trade  or profession depends on the availability
of a  "safe" working  environment. Right  to life means life
with dignity.  The primary  responsibility fro ensuring such
safety and  dignity through  suitable legislation,  and	 the
creation of  a mechanism  for its  enforcement,	 is  of	 the
legislature and	 the executive.	 When, however, instances of
sexual harassment  resulting  in  violation  of	 fundamental
rights of  women workers  under
Articles  14
, 19
and
21
are
brought before us for redress under
Article 32
, an effective
redressal requires  that some guidelines should be laid down
for the	 protection of	these rights to fill the legislative
vacuum.
The notice	 of the	 petition was  given to the State of
Rajasthan and  the Union  of India.  The  learned  Solicitor
General	 appeared  for	the  Union  of	India  and  rendered
valuable assistance  in the  true spirit of a Law Officer to
help us	 find a	 proper solution  to this  social problem of
considerable magnitude.	 In addition  to Ms. Meenakshi Arora
and Ms.	 Naina	Kapur  who  assisted  the  Court  with	full
commitment, Shri  Fali S.  Nariman appeared as Amicus Curiae
and rendered  great assistance. We place on record our great
appreciation for  every counsel who appeared in the case and
rendered the  needed  assistance  to  the  Court  which	 has
enabled us  to deal  with this	unusual matter in the manner
considered appropriate for a cause of this nature.
Apart from
Article 32
of the Constitution of India, we
may refer  to some  other provision  which envisage judicial
intervention for  eradication  of  this	 social	 evil.	Some

JUDGMENT

Mukundakam Sharma, J.
1. This appeal arises out of the judgment and order passed on January 31, 2003 by the learned Additional District Judge in Suit No. 121/2000 dismissing the said suit.
2. The suit was instituted by the appellant as the plaintiff against the respondents-defendants. In the cause title of the plaint, the appellant-plaintiff described itself as follows:-
"M/s. Miraj Marketing Corporation (Regd) 

 206, IInd Floor, Miraj Plaza, 

 East Patel Nagar,  

 Delhi-8"
[Through its authorised representative] 

Mr.Amitabh Sharma

The original plaint filed by the plaintiff was amended subsequently and in the amended plaint also the appellant-plaintiff described itself as above. In paragraph 1 of the plaint the plaintiff stated that the plaintiff is a proprietorship firm having its office at the aforementioned address. The said suit was instituted by the appellant-plaintiff seeking for a decree for recovery of Rs. 4,34,600/- along with pendente lite and future interest from the date of institution of the suit till realisation.
3. In the written statement filed by the defendants, certain preliminary objections were raised. One of the said objections was that the plaint had not been signed or verified, or the suit had not been filed by a duly authorised person and that Mr. Amitabh Sharma was neither the proprietor nor a duly authorised representative of the plaintiff firm and as such Mr. Amitabh Sharma was not competent or empowered to file, sign and verify the plaint and hence the said suit of the plaintiff was liable to be dismissed on the said ground.
4. On the pleadings of the parties, the trial court framed the following issues:-
1. Whether the plaintiff is entitled to the suit amount? OPD.
2. Whether the suit of the plaintiff is barred by
section 69(2)
of the Partnership Act? OPD.
3. Whether the suit of the plaintiff is barred U/O 13
Rule 10 CPC
? OPD.
4. Whether the suit of the plaintiff is not signed and verified by a duly authorised person? OPD.
5. Whether the plaintiff is entitled to the interest, if so, at what rate? OPP.
6. Relief.
5. During the course of trial the appellant-plaintiff examined Shri Ajay Gogia as PW-1 and filed his examination-in-chief by way of an affidavit. The appellant-plaintiff also examined Shri A.K. Pandey as PW-2 and also filed his examination-in-chief through an affidavit whereas the respondents-defendants examined Mr.Sanjeev Kapil as DW-1.
6. In the verification of the affidavit filed by way of evidence filed by Shri Ajay Gogia as PW-1, it was stated thus:-
"Verification:
Verified on this 30th day of July 2002, that the contents of the above affidavit is (are) true and correct to the best of my knowledge and nothing material has been concealed there from."
Similar verification was also done in the affidavit filed by way of evidence by Shri A.K. Pandey as follows:-
"Verification:
Verified on this 30th day of July 2002 that the contents of the above affidavit is true and correct to the best of my knowledge and nothing material has been concealed there from."
3. The learned Additional District Judge thereafter heard the arguments in the said suit and by judgment and order passed on January 31, 2003 he dismissed the said suit filed by the plaintiff in the light of the evidence recorded by him as against Issues No. 1, 4 and 5. Issues No. 1 and 5 were taken up first. While discussing the said issues, the learned trial court referred to the aforesaid verifications appended to the affidavits by way of evidence by the witnesses of the plaintiff. In the light of the said verifications in both the affidavits it was held that it could not be said that the verification of the two affidavits was in compliance with
Order 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure
. The trial court further held that the affidavits/evidence filed by the plaintiff was not proper and legal evidence and no reliance could be placed safely on them and, therefore, the said affidavit could not be read in evidence. It was also held that as the plaintiff had failed to lead any evidence therefore there was no evidence on record, and consequently the plaintiff had failed to discharge the onus. The said issues were decided in favor of the defendants and against the plaintiff.
4. So far issue No. 4 is concerned, it was held by the learned trial court that the present suit had been brought in the name of M/s. Miraj Marketing Corporation through one authorised representative Mr. Amitabh Sharma who was not the proprietor and no authority of Mr. Amitabh Sharma was proved on record. Mr. A.K. Pandey, PW-1, filed affidavit by way of evidence wherein he had stated that he was the proprietor of the plaintiff firm and that the plaintiff was a sole proprietorship firm. He had not stated in his affidavit that the plaint was signed and verified by him.
5. It was submitted by the counsel for the plaintiff during the course of his arguments before the trial court that the plaint had been filed by the proprietor, Shri A.K. Pandey, on behalf of the proprietorship firm.
As there was no statement as to who was the proprietor of the firm in the plaint nor it was mentioned as to who had signed the plaint, it was held by the trial court that a proprietorship firm is not a legal entity and, therefore, the suit could not be brought in the firm's name. The suit was accordingly dismissed.
Being aggrieved by the said judgment, the present appeal is filed on which we have heard the learned counsel appearing for the parties and gone through the record.
6. It was submitted by the learned counsel appearing for the appellant that the verifications/affidavits filed by way of evidence were in the nature of evidence and the said affidavits were properly verified as required under Rule 3 of
Order XIX of the Code of Civil Procedure
. It was submitted by him that both the deponents, namely, Shri Ajay Gogia and Shri A.K. Pandey, in their verifications in the affidavits had stated that the contents of the affidavits were true and correct to the best of their knowledge and, therefore, the said verifications in both the affidavits satisfied the requirements of Rule 3 of
Order XIX of the Code of Civil Procedure
.
7.
Order XIX of the Code of Civil Procedure
permits a court to receive evidence by way of affidavit for proving particular fact or facts. Affidavits are not included in the definition of 'evidence' in
section 3
of the Evidence Act and can be used as evidence only if, for sufficient reasons, a court passes an order to that effect under Order XIX Rule 1 or 2
of the Code of Civil Procedure
. As to how an affidavit is to be filed is also set out in Rule 3 of the said Order XIX. It is provided therein that the affidavits shall be confined to such facts as the deponent is able of his own knowledge to prove, except on interlocutory applications, on which statements of his belief may be admitted provided that the grounds thereof are stated.
8.
In the case entitled
A.K.K. Nambiar v. Union of India
, , it was held by the Supreme Court that in the absence of proper verification, affidavits could not be admitted in evidence.
We may also advert to the judgment of this court reported as
D.N. Gupta v. Jaswant Singh
, , it was held that where an affidavit seeking to leave to defend application is not properly verified it cannot be allowed to be amended but the deponent may be given an opportunity to file another affidavit.
In the case of
Musebhai Jivanbhai Jivani v. Special Land Acquisition Officer
, (1999-2) 19 Gujarat Law Journal 108, the Division
